removal_suggestion: Re-present the requirement indirectly as an operational scenario: define success through the absence of a separation between any two designated core components, and describe non-core components as ordinary relay-capable components rather than explicitly calling them optional supplemental Steiner vertices.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Recognizes the task as a minimum Steiner tree and applies Dreyfus-Wagner-style subset DP over the at-most-ten core components.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: all core components are synchronized ... either directly or transitively through intermediate components; the remaining components may be used or ignored

common_affordance: The statement directly exposes a minimum-cost connected subgraph spanning a small set of required terminals, with arbitrary non-core relay vertices allowed.

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: It computes shortest paths and appears to solve the terminal metric closure, which can overpay because several terminal paths may share a useful intermediate Steiner component and edge set.
Its shortest-path-based approach has the same metric-closure weakness: independently optimal terminal-to-terminal paths need not form the minimum shared protocol network.

It applies Kruskal-style processing to the full graph rather than solving the minimum connected subgraph problem restricted to spanning all core terminals; ordinary MST processing does not correctly account for optional relay vertices and the terminal-only objective.

recommended_edit: Replace the explicit synchronization wording with an indirect operational formulation in which selected protocols make the core set mutually reachable, while describing all components uniformly as possible relays; avoid explicitly naming the supplemental components and the direct/transitive Steiner-tree interpretation.
